newsitem.title: UK: BIT to sell EFM stake in restructuring.
newsitem.headline: BIT to sell EFM stake in restructuring.

text.p: The British Investment Trust Plc (BIT) said it would sell its 32.5 percent stake in Edinburgh Fund Managers via a institutional placing and share buy-back by Edinburgh.

It said the sale was part of a restructuring by BIT following a decision by 84.9 percent shareholder the British Coal Pension Schemes to that it was no longer appropriate for BCPS to hold such a significant proportion of their assets via a quoted investment trust.

It said a successor equity unit trust would be available to BIT minority shareholders, and that the proposed placing and buy-back had received the support of the major clients and management of Edinburgh.

About 7.6 million Edinburgh ordinary shares are to be conditionally placed with a spread of institutional and other investors. HSBC James Capel and Panmure Gordon & Co. will act as joint lead managers and Schroders and Flemings will act as co-lead managers to the placing.
The remaining 2.6 million shares will be bought back by Edinburgh at the placing price.
Marketing will commence today and it is expected that the placing will take place on March 14, when the placing price will be announced.
The BIT management contract with Edinburgh will be terminated and BIT has agreed to pay Edinburgh some 2.5 million stg as compensation. It will be paid by BCPS.
Edinburgh is expected to manage the BCPS's Premier and Globe portfolios worth 383 million stg at the end of February, as well as the successor trust.

The loss of management fees from BIT and the revised terms of the Premier and Globe portfolios would result in a reduction in Edinburgh's annual revenues of about 2.4 million stg, while potential revenues from the successor trust could be up to 1.6 million stg a year.
The contribution to Edinburgh's revenues will depend on the number of BIT minority shareholders who choose to remain invested in the trust.

The overall effect of the buy-back combined with the reconstruction of BIT and revised terms for Premier and Globe would have resulted in a reduction in Edinburgh's earnings per share of between one and 10 percent, depending on the extent of participation in the successor trust.

The loss of BIT's portfolio would have reduced proforma funds under management to approximately 6.7 billion from about 7.6 billion. The buy-back will be financed out of Edinburgh's existing cash resources.
The statement said the objectives of the reconstruction were to eliminate BIT's discount to net asset value and to create greater liquidity for BCPS.
BIT's minority shareholders will exchange their ordinary Shares in BIT for units in a new authorised equity unit trust managed by Edinburgh, without incurring an initial charge.
An asset allocation policy similar to the current one is expected to be followed.
